metadata.title: Caching Pixels You've Already Seen.
metadata.purpose: Take apart what actually happens when a computer-use agent resends the same screenshot: by default the API is stateless and re-tokenizes every image, and cache_control ephemeral is a request-level opt-in that trades permanence for a ninety-percent cut on repeats. Explain the machinery, name the trade-off, honor the limits.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B04 (50-turn task, 5 unique desktop states A-E: 100,000 tokens uncached vs 10,000 cached)

beats.narration_text: Liam, in for Bear. You'd assume a screenshot Claude has already seen costs nothing to resend. It doesn't. The API re-tokenizes every image fresh — no identity check on pixels — unless you explicitly flag it as one it has seen before.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'If Claude already saw this screenshot, does sending it again cost nothing?', hesitates on 'nothing', corrects to 'the same', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('nothing' -> 'the same') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A computer-use agent snaps a screenshot every turn. Fifty turns, fifty images. Most of them are identical — the dialog hasn't moved, the progress bar is still crawling — but the API doesn't check. It re-tokenizes each screenshot from scratch, roughly two thousand tokens a pop. Thirty-five of the fifty turns bill the API for pixels it already tokenized once. Here's what's actually happening: the default optimized for statelessness — every request stands alone, no server-side memory to leak or invalidate. Clean design. For a nearly-static desktop, statelessness is a tax.

shot.new_visual_element: 50 turn-slots in a row, a dialog and a progress bar shown unchanged across several, 35 marked as repeats, a token counter climbing beside them

production_viz.label: The naive loop, unpriced
production_viz.mechanic: 50 small rectangles in a horizontal row on cream, representing turns. Two small icons (a dialog box, a progress bar) sit above a cluster of identical-looking turns to sell 'nothing changed'. 35 of the 50 rectangles shade identically (INK_SOFT, marked 'same image'); 15 are outlined in teal ('new state'). A token counter beside the row climbs step by step toward 70,000 tokens spent re-reading repeats.

beats.narration_text: Make it concrete. Across those fifty turns, the desktop only ever cycles through five distinct states — call them A through E. The API can't tell that turn twelve is pixel-identical to turn three; there's no server-side identity index behind the scenes. It just bills the full two thousand tokens per screenshot, fifty times over. One hundred thousand tokens to describe a screen that actually changed five times. The trade-off is visible: statelessness bought simplicity — it cost you every repeat.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - a 50-frame filmstrip, five states A-E repeating, every frame billed the same, a counter climbing to 100,000 tokens

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - the unoptimized bill
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A 50-frame filmstrip scrolls across cream; each frame is labelled with one of five states (A-E) repeating in sequence, every frame the same terracotta 'billed full price' color regardless of repeats. A counter beside it climbs to '100,000 tokens'. THIS EXACT FILMSTRIP RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: Here's the actual machinery. One field on the image block: cache_control, type ephemeral. Flag a screenshot the first time its exact pixels arrive, and the API stores a tokenized representation of it. Send the same pixels flagged again, and it's a hit — the API recognizes them, skips the re-tokenization, bills close to zero. The payload you send doesn't change. What changes is whether the API has to do the tokenizing work twice. You opted in per image; the API opted in to remembering.

shot.new_visual_element: The cache_control JSON field appearing on an image block; a first-sighting screenshot flagged, a repeat of it landing as a HIT

production_viz.label: One field: cache_control ephemeral
production_viz.mechanic: A JSON image block on cream; the line 'cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}' types itself in beside it. Below, two small screenshot icons: the first, labelled 'MISS - full price', in terracotta; the second, identical, labelled 'HIT - next to nothing', in teal.

beats.narration_text: Back to the fifty-turn task. Five unique states, five cache misses, forty-five hits. Ten thousand tokens instead of one hundred thousand — ninety percent off. Judge it honestly, though. This is the screenshot case only. It doesn't cover the full caching protocol, the minimum cacheable size, or the eviction rules. And the cache itself is ephemeral by design — that's literally the name of the flag. Switch API keys, or let the task idle too long, and the very next screenshot is a miss again, whether or not the pixels actually changed. This works if you value throughput. It fails if you assumed the memory was permanent.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same 50-frame filmstrip, now 5 miss-frames in terracotta and 45 hit-frames in teal, counter dropping to 10,000 tokens; a struck card noting scope limits

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - cut down, and the scope limit
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 FILMSTRIP RETURNS, identical, then recolors: the 5 first-sightings of each state stay terracotta ('MISS'), the 45 repeats turn teal ('HIT'). The counter drops from '100,000' to '10,000 tokens', a '90% saved' badge appears. Beside it, a small card: 'not the full protocol' and 'not permanent', both in ink — marked as scope limits, not struck as false.

beats.narration_text: Claude doesn't know a screenshot repeats until you tell it to remember one — and that memory only lasts until the picture, or the session, changes.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to understand how the Anthropic Messages API treats image identity across requests. A computer-use agent takes a screenshot every turn of a fifty-turn task, and thirty-five of them are pixel-identical to earlier ones. Without cache flags, at two thousand tokens per screenshot, that burns one hundred thousand tokens describing five actual desktop states. Walk me through what cache_control ephemeral changes, what a miss versus a hit costs, and where the ephemeral cache actually lives — session, key, or account. Then go deeper: if one pixel shifts — antialiasing jitter, a blinking cursor, a clock tick — does the cache still hit, or does the pixel-diff force a miss? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how the Anthropic Messages API treats image identity across requests. A computer-use agent takes a screenshot every turn of a fifty-turn task, and roughly thirty-five of those screenshots are pixel-identical to earlier turns. Without any cache flags, at ~2000 tokens per screenshot, the agent burns ~100,000 tokens describing five actual desktop states. Walk me through, step by step: (1) what changes when I add cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'} to each image block, (2) what a cache miss versus a cache hit costs in tokens, and (3) where the ephemeral cache lives — per session, per API key, per account. Then give me two failure modes where the cache silently disappears mid-task.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: If the screenshot changes by a single pixel — antialiasing jitter, a blinking cursor, a clock tick — does the cache still hit, or does the pixel-diff force a miss? What's the actual comparison function inside the cache?
